Let’s dive into Chapter 1: Rethinking Progress—Why Creating Something New Matters Most.
When you think about building something truly transformative, it all starts with a pretty simple—yet powerful—idea. There’s a big difference between just making small improvements, and actually inventing something brand new. Most of us, when we picture progress, imagine tweaking what already exists. Maybe you copy a good idea, make it a bit better, and share it with more people. That’s what you might call going from “one to n”—taking something familiar and multiplying it.
But then there’s the real leap: going from “zero to one.” This is when you create something that no one’s ever seen before. It’s this kind of breakthrough that actually shapes the future.
And this isn’t just a theory. This difference—between imitation and true invention—actually influences how we, our teams, and even entire societies approach innovation. Sure, copying what works can make things more efficient and help us grow. But let’s be honest—it rarely leads to those game-changing breakthroughs. The real magic, and the real value, comes from that moment when someone dares to invent, to step into the unknown and bring something completely new to life.
Think for a moment about globalization versus technological innovation. Globalization is all about spreading existing ideas and tech around the world—basically taking what works in one place and replicating it everywhere else. It makes things more accessible, but also a bit more uniform. Now, technological innovation? That’s where the excitement is. It’s about coming up with solutions, products, and ways of thinking that simply didn’t exist before. That’s what makes the world not just bigger, but richer and more interesting.
Here’s something to pay attention to—if you want to build a lasting company, you’ve got to shift your mindset. Instead of asking, “How can I do what everyone else is doing, but just a little better?” try asking, “What valuable thing is nobody else even trying?” That question isn’t easy to answer. It means you have to look past what’s already out there, challenge the usual assumptions, and search for those hidden opportunities that others might miss.
In real life, the most successful startups don’t just jump into crowded markets and fight for a tiny slice of what’s already there. No—they create new markets, or they change the rules so much that they’re suddenly the only game in town. Think about the early days of personal computers. It wasn’t about making a better typewriter. It was about inventing a whole new way for people to interact with information. Or the first social networks—they didn’t just improve on how we communicated. They created brand new ways for us to connect.
Of course, this approach isn’t without risk. Creating something new is always uncertain. There’s no roadmap, no formula, and sometimes, not even a clear demand. But the rewards—both in impact and in value—are so much greater than just following the crowd.
If you want to foster real innovation, you’ve got to start valuing originality over imitation. That means questioning what everyone takes for granted, looking for secrets or overlooked truths, and having the courage to act on them. It also means realizing that the best opportunities are often the ones nobody else even sees, and that sometimes, the right path is the one that goes against the grain.
So, here’s the key takeaway: building the future really comes down to “zero to one” progress—the act of creating new value, new products, and new ways of thinking. That’s the work of true entrepreneurs. They’re the ones who shape the world, not just compete in it.
